extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/natural history/natural science (readers interested in teleology, instinct, and explanations in biology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how to explain natural phenomena by final (teleological) causes versus efficient (mechanical) causes, and on the nature and classification of instinct and mechanical tendencies in animals. The chapter compares explanatory strategies, gives definitions, and supplies illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer final causes in organised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: In the investigation of organised nature we are entirely referred to final causes; we everywhere seek for these and explain everything from them. In explaining the origin of the parts we again look for [efficient causes] no more, but are satisfied with the final causes alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used especially for explaining the origin and arrangement of organs and structures (examples: corolla protecting pistil/stamina, flowers preparing pollen/germs, essential oils protecting anthers). Final causes are the appropriate principle for studying organised (living) systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat efficient causes as subordinate/tools within organised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficient causes, on the contrary, assume only a quite subordinate position as the mere tools of the final causes... of the actually efficient causes which bring about, for example, the eye, the ear, the brain, we know absolutely nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient causes may be sought in physiology but often are unknown or less informative; at most general principles (e.g., larger part requires stronger artery) may be obtainable. Do not expect efficient causes alone to fully explain purposive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: In physiological functions final causes are often more instructive than efficient causes
rubrics_metrics.description: In explaining the physiological functions we certainly look about for the efficient causes, though for the most part in vain; ... the final cause is far more important and more to the point than the efficient; therefore, if the former alone is known we are instructed and satisfied with regard to the principal matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: even without knowing the efficient cause of blood circulation, knowing the final causes (oxidation in lungs; nourishment) yields much explanatory light. Prioritize teleological understanding when it clarifies function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer efficient causes in unorganised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: That in unorganised nature the final causes entirely withdraw into the background, so that an explanation from them alone is here no longer valid, but the efficient causes are rather indispensably required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For physical, geological, and other unorganised phenomena look to mechanical and efficient explanations (examples/contra: why sea is salt); final causes in this domain are ambiguous and often misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final causes provide sufficient/perfect explanation within their sphere; efficient causes give only relative explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every efficient cause always ultimately rests upon something that cannot be fathomed, a force of nature, i.e., a qualitas occulta, and, therefore, it can only give a relative explanation; while the final cause within its sphere affords a sufficient and perfect explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the explanatory scope: teleological accounts can be self-sufficient for purposes/functions, whereas mechanical accounts may leave ultimate 'how' unexplained. Both perspectives have value but differ in completeness depending on the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal explanation identifies both efficient and final causes separately
rubrics_metrics.description: We are only perfectly content when we know both the efficient cause... and the final cause... at once and yet separately, as their concurrence, their wonderful working together, then surprises us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for dual knowledge where possible: knowing both the mechanism and the end gives the fullest understanding; though in practice this twofold knowledge is seldom attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: External design (end in one individual, means in another) is acceptable when participants belong to the same species or when species maintenance depends on it
rubrics_metrics.description: When the end lies in one individual and the means in another... it remains unquestionable so long as the two belong to the same species, indeed it then becomes the more striking. When the individual that affords essential help to another belongs to an entirely different species, and even to another kingdom of nature, we will doubt this external design... unless it is evident that the maintenance of the species depends upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological explanations for reciprocal adaptations (e.g., insect pollination of plants) especially where coevolution and species-level maintenance provide clear functional dependence; be cautious invoking design across unrelated taxa without such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using external design as physico-theological proof; look for ateleological counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one desires to misuse the external design ... there are in this class enough examples in contrarium, thus ateleological instances, to derange his conception. One of the strongest is presented by the unsuitableness of sea-water for drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological arguments that are used to infer divine or optimal design must address counterexamples (apparent maladaptations) and not ignore cases where purposive explanations seem implausible or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of instinct (criterion for classifying actions as instinctive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct is a character which is only set in motion by a quite specially determined motive, and on this account the action that proceeds from it is always exactly of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify behaviour as instinctive when (a) it is elicited only by a narrowly specified external trigger (season, material, location), and (b) the resulting action is stereotyped and uniform (examples: nest-building, spider web spinning, specific egg-laying sites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation vs instinct: difference of degree, not kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The motive also only acts under the assumption of an inner tendency, i.e., a definite quality of will which is called its character. The motive ... only gives to this a definite direction—individualises it for the concrete case. So also instinct... waits for some external circumstance necessarily demanded for its action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'motivation' and 'instinct' as points along a continuum: both involve inner tendencies (character) but differ in breadth of triggering conditions and flexibility; analyse specific cases to determine position on this continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation implies broader knowledge and higher intellect; instinct requires limited intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Being determined by mere motivation presupposes a certain width of the sphere of knowledge, and consequently a more fully developed intellect: therefore it is peculiar to the higher animals, quite pre-eminently, however, to man; while being determined by instinct only demands as much intellect as is necessary to apprehend the one quite specially determined motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing behavior, use the breadth of stimulus-response mapping and evidence of problem-solving/adaptation as indicators of cognitive complexity: flexible motivated actions suggest higher intellect, narrow instinctive actions suggest lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical tendencies demonstrate purposive action without conscious knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical tendencies of animals show most clearly that creatures can work with the greatest decision and definiteness towards an end which they do not know... Precisely so, however, does organising nature work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like bird's nest, spider's web, bee hive, ant-lion pit to argue that teleology (goal-directedness) does not require consciousness of the end; mechanical tendencies provide analogies to organismic purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive actions are not purely automatic; intellect adapts particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct gives the universal, the rule; the intellect the particular, the application, in that it directs the detail of the execution, in which therefore the work of these animals clearly adapts itself to the circumstances of the existing case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cases for evidence of repair, modification, or context-sensitive adjustments (examples: caterpillar repairing web, bees adapting hive after damage, ants moving larvae when nest becomes damp) to show interplay of instinct and limited intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy between insect societies and organisms to understand functional subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: In the insect society, as in the animal organism, the vita propria of each part is subordinated to the life of the whole, and the care for the whole precedes that for particular existence; indeed the latter is only conditionally willed, the former unconditionally; therefore the individuals are even sacrificed occasionally for the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting social insect behaviour (division of labour, self-sacrifice, caste roles), consider organismic analogies: individuals function like organs; evaluate behaviours in light of the maintenance of the whole (examples: ants building dam with bodies, drones killed when useless, queen's egg-laying vs workers' tasks).
